text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: the most likely primary fault is a heat-exchange and metering problem centered on a dirty outdoor condenser coil combined with either unstable refrigerant flow through the electronic expansion valve or a refrigerant-side fault causing evaporator freeze protection to intervene. The reported CH21 code, the noisy expansion valve, the very poor delivered cooling performance, and compressor short cycling all point toward the indoor coil temperature dropping into a protection threshold rather than the system maintaining normal superheat and stable run time.
- Code interpretation: CH21 is commonly reported in Daikin field discussions and service references as an indoor heat-exchanger thermistor or freeze-protection related fault family on certain Daikin commercial/light commercial platforms, though exact meaning depends on the indoor unit series and controller. On a 2019 SkyAir, that makes the code highly relevant because a bad coil sensor, out-of-range thermistor reading, or actual evaporator icing event can all force short cycling and weak cooling.
- Component failure analysis: the noisy expansion valve is not normal background operation if staff specifically noticed it. On Daikin inverter systems, the electronic expansion valve can click or buzz lightly during stepping, but pronounced noise paired with only a 5°F supply-to-return split suggests the valve may be hunting, restricted, underfed by low charge, or being commanded incorrectly due to bad sensor input. A dusty outdoor coil at 92°F ambient also raises condensing pressure, reduces heat rejection, and can aggravate compressor cycling and poor capacity.
- Performance analysis: a healthy comfort-cooling system in these conditions would usually show roughly a 16°F to 22°F return-to-supply temperature drop once stabilized, assuming normal airflow and humidity load. A measured split of only 5°F is severe underperformance and is not explained by a recently replaced filter alone.
- Age considerations: a 2019 Daikin SkyAir is not old enough to assume end-of-life compressor wear first. At this age, common causes are maintenance-related airflow/coil fouling, thermistor drift, EEV issues, charge loss from a small leak, or control-board/sensor logic faults rather than catastrophic compressor failure.
- Safety concerns: refrigerant diagnosis and any charge correction require EPA Section 608-certified handling. Electrical testing inside the outdoor unit exposes technicians to high voltage and inverter components that can retain charge. If the office serves vulnerable occupants, inadequate cooling at 92°F ambient can become a health risk.
- Confidence: 76%.
- Data Needed
- Full model numbers for indoor and outdoor units, plus controller type, because Daikin code definitions vary by series.
- Suction pressure, liquid pressure if applicable, line temperatures, calculated superheat/subcooling, and compressor amp draw after 10 to 15 minutes of operation.
- Thermistor resistance or temperature readings for indoor coil, return air, and outdoor ambient sensors compared against Daikin service manual charts.
- Photos of the outdoor coil condition, indoor evaporator coil, drain pan, and controller display showing CH21.
- Static pressure, blower speed setting, and confirmation that all supply/return grilles and dampers are open.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Electronic expansion valve malfunction or unstable control command is the leading alternative within the primary diagnosis cluster. This is ruled in by the reported valve noise, poor cooling, and short cycling. It is not yet proven because low refrigerant charge or false thermistor data can make a healthy valve behave erratically.
- Low refrigerant charge from a leak is high likelihood. It fits weak cooling, possible evaporator freeze events, and compressor short cycling on protection. It is strengthened if suction pressure is low and superheat is high. It is weakened if subcooling and sight indicators, where applicable, remain normal and leak search is negative.
- Indoor evaporator thermistor fault is high-to-moderate likelihood. CH21 strongly keeps this in play. A sensor reading colder than actual can prematurely cycle the compressor and mimic freeze protection even when the coil is not iced. This is a known failure pattern on inverter-driven ducted and cassette systems across several brands, including Daikin.
- Dirty outdoor condenser coil causing high head pressure and capacity loss is moderate likelihood. The customer specifically reports the coil is dusty and ambient is 92°F. That absolutely reduces efficiency and can trigger protective cycling, but by itself it usually does not create only a 5°F split unless the fouling is substantial or combined with another fault.
- Airflow restriction across the indoor coil is moderate likelihood despite the filter being recently replaced. A new filter does not rule out a dirty evaporator coil, collapsed flex duct, closed dampers, blower wheel fouling, or incorrect fan speed. Low airflow can cause coil icing and freeze-related codes.
- Compressor inverter/control issue is lower likelihood. Daikin SkyAir systems use inverter logic that can short cycle if the board sees abnormal sensor data or current draw. However, with no auto-detected compressor-specific code and a reported noisy expansion valve, metering/sensing remains more likely than a failing compressor.
- Reversing valve leakage or partial bypass is lower likelihood if this is a heat pump model. It can reduce cooling capacity dramatically, but it usually presents with abnormal line temperatures and not specifically with CH21.
- Duct leakage or return bypass is lower likelihood but still possible. If supply air is mixing back into the return near the unit, measured split can appear low. That would not explain the expansion valve noise or CH21 as well as refrigerant/sensor faults do.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Recover the exact Daikin fault history from the wired controller or service checker, not just the current display. The shop must document active and stored codes, including CH21 occurrence count and timestamp. Expected cost: $120 to $220 for 1.0 to 1.5 diagnostic hours.
- Measure return-air dry bulb, supply-air dry bulb, indoor wet bulb if possible, and outdoor ambient after 10 to 15 minutes of stable operation. At 92°F ambient, a properly operating office unit should generally exceed a 5°F split by a wide margin. Tools: calibrated digital psychrometer and probe thermometers. Expected cost: included in diagnostic hour.
- Check indoor airflow and external static pressure. Tools: manometer, fan table, and blower speed verification. Expected readings depend on indoor unit type, but airflow should be near design cfm per ton and static should not exceed the air handler’s rated limit. Cost: $80 to $180 if billed separately.
- Inspect and clean the outdoor condenser coil before final refrigerant conclusions. A dirty coil distorts head pressure readings. Tools: coil cleaner approved for microchannel/fin type, low-pressure rinse, fin comb if needed. Cost: $150 to $350 depending on access and coil condition.
- Verify refrigerant circuit operation with gauges or manufacturer-approved pressure/temperature methods for the specific refrigerant used by this 2019 SkyAir, commonly R-410A on many models. Record suction saturation, liquid saturation if service ports/configuration allow, line temperatures, superheat, subcooling, and compressor amperage. Cost: $180 to $350 diagnostic if not included.
- Test indoor coil thermistor and related sensors against Daikin resistance-temperature charts from the service manual. A sensor out of tolerance or intermittently open/shorted can directly cause CH21-type faults. Tools: ohmmeter, temperature probe, service manual chart. Cost: $120 to $250.
- Command and observe EEV operation through service mode if supported. Listen for stepping, verify coil resistance, and compare target versus actual operating behavior. If the valve is hunting due to bad data, sensor values will expose it. Cost: $150 to $300.
- Inspect the indoor coil for frost/ice, blower wheel contamination, drain issues, and signs of oil residue at flare joints or braze points. Oil staining is a strong leak clue. Cost: usually included in diagnostic time.
- If low charge is suspected, perform an electronic leak search and, if needed, nitrogen pressure test after proper recovery. Refrigerant handling must be by EPA Section 608-certified personnel. Cost: $250 to $700 depending on leak complexity.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- “Can you show me the exact Daikin code history and tell me what CH21 means for my specific indoor unit model?” They must identify the model-specific code definition, not guess from memory. Red flag: “Codes are generic” or “it just means low Freon.”
- “What were the return and supply temperatures, indoor wet bulb, outdoor ambient, and the stabilized temperature split after the unit ran?” They should show measured numbers, not “it felt warm.” Red flag: no psychrometric data on a cooling complaint.
- “What were suction conditions, line temperatures, superheat, subcooling, and compressor amp draw before and after coil cleaning?” This exposes whether they actually diagnosed the refrigerant circuit. Red flag: adding refrigerant without documenting these readings.
- “Did you ohm-check the indoor coil thermistor and compare it to the Daikin chart, since CH21 may point to a sensor or freeze-protection issue?” Red flag: replacing the expansion valve first without validating sensor inputs.
- “How did you verify airflow — static pressure, blower speed, evaporator cleanliness, and damper position?” Red flag: assuming airflow is fine because the filter is new.
- Specific data they must show you includes a photo of the controller code, a written pressure/temperature sheet, thermistor readings, amp draw, and before/after coil condition.
- Red flag responses include “these Daikins always need gas,” “we don’t check static on package systems,” and “the valve is noisy so we’ll just replace it.”

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand what your testing showed on this 2019 Daikin SkyAir, especially with the CH21 code, the 5-degree temperature split, and the short cycling.”
- Phrasing: keep it curious and specific. Say, “Help me understand how you separated a sensor issue from an expansion-valve or refrigerant-charge issue.”
- Example dialogue: “Could you walk me through the exact meaning of CH21 on my model and show me where you found it in the Daikin service information?”
- Example dialogue: “What were the return and supply temperatures after the unit stabilized, and what indoor/outdoor conditions were you using when you judged performance?”
- Example dialogue: “Before recommending parts, did you clean the dusty outdoor coil and then recheck pressures, superheat, subcooling, and amp draw?”
- Example dialogue: “Since staff reported a noisy expansion valve, what test proved the valve itself is faulty rather than reacting to a bad thermistor or low charge?”
- Example dialogue: “Can you show me the thermistor readings against the Daikin resistance chart and the airflow/static measurements?”
- Body language: stay calm, take notes, and pause after each answer. A competent technician will usually become more precise when they see you value measured data.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say, “I’m not questioning your skill — I just approve repairs based on test results, and I’d like to understand the basis for the recommendation.”
- Exit strategy: “Please email me the diagnostic findings, model-specific code definition, and a line-item quote. I’d like to review it before authorizing refrigerant or major parts.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Basic professional diagnostic visit with Daikin code retrieval, temperature split check, and visual inspection is typically $120 to $250.
- Outdoor coil cleaning on a light commercial split or SkyAir condenser usually runs $150 to $350, more if access is difficult or the coil is heavily impacted.
- Airflow/static and blower verification typically adds $80 to $180 if not included in the diagnostic package.
- Thermistor testing and replacement, if a sensor is confirmed bad, often totals $180 to $450 depending on access and exact indoor unit type. The sensor itself is often relatively inexpensive; labor drives the bill.
- EEV diagnostic labor can run $150 to $300. If the electronic expansion valve assembly is actually failed, total repair can range roughly $700 to $1,800 depending on refrigerant recovery, brazing/access, board calibration, and refrigerant recharge.
- Refrigerant leak search and minor charge correction can range from $350 to $900. If a leak is found and repaired, total cost can exceed that depending on location and refrigerant quantity.
- Compressor or inverter board work is the expensive branch, often $1,500 to $4,000, but nothing in your current data justifies jumping there first.
- Fair pricing sequence for this case is diagnostic plus coil cleaning first, then retest. A reasonable first authorization is often $300 to $600 total for proper diagnosis and cleaning. Approving an EEV replacement or refrigerant add without measured data would be premature.
- Overcharge markers include flatly charging “system recharge” without leak testing, billing premium refrigerant rates with no weight documented, or quoting an expansion valve solely because it is noisy.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts cannon indicator: the shop immediately blames the expansion valve because staff heard noise, without checking thermistors, airflow, and coil cleanliness first.
- Diagnostic shortcut: they attach gauges, glance at pressures on a dirty condenser, and sell refrigerant without cleaning the coil or documenting indoor conditions.
- Price gouging red flag: charging several hundred dollars for “code clearing and reset” when CH21 requires actual root-cause diagnosis.
- Another red flag is saying the new filter proves airflow is fine. Filters are only one part of airflow; evaporator fouling, blower wheel buildup, and duct restrictions are common hidden causes.
- Be cautious if they refuse to provide superheat, subcooling, amp draw, or thermistor readings. On a Daikin inverter system, those are core diagnostic data points.
- Be cautious if they recommend compressor replacement before proving the compressor is being commanded correctly and is not simply shutting down on protection.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: a full diagnostic that includes Daikin code history retrieval, outdoor coil cleaning, airflow/static verification, thermistor testing, and refrigerant performance measurements after cleaning.
- Approve immediately: leak search only if the post-cleaning readings indicate low charge or abnormal superheat/subcooling consistent with refrigerant loss.
- Reject outright: “top off the refrigerant and see what happens” without leak evaluation and documented operating data.
- Reject outright: expansion valve replacement based only on noise, with no sensor validation and no refrigerant circuit measurements.
- Get a second opinion if the shop cannot define CH21 for your exact model, cannot show measured data, or wants to replace major components before cleaning and retesting the dirty condenser.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: your Daikin SkyAir uses an outdoor condensing unit and an indoor coil connected by refrigerant lines. The compressor moves refrigerant, the outdoor coil rejects heat, and the expansion valve meters refrigerant into the indoor coil where it absorbs heat from office air.
- Why the 5°F split matters: in cooling mode, the indoor coil should remove both sensible heat and moisture. A 5°F drop means the system is moving air but not absorbing enough heat, or the measured air is being mixed or bypassed. That is a major performance deficit.
- Failure mechanism for a dirty outdoor coil: dust blocks heat rejection, raises condensing temperature and pressure, reduces efficiency, and can trigger protective shutdowns. In hot weather, this gets worse quickly.
- Failure mechanism for low airflow: if not enough warm air crosses the indoor coil, the coil temperature can plunge below freezing. Ice forms, airflow drops further, and the system may trip freeze protection or short cycle.
- Failure mechanism for low refrigerant charge: too little refrigerant can starve the evaporator, causing low suction pressure, high superheat, poor capacity, and possible icing. Simply adding refrigerant without finding the leak is not a proper repair.
- Failure mechanism for a bad thermistor: if the indoor coil sensor falsely reports very cold coil temperature, the control board may cycle the compressor off to prevent icing even when the coil is not actually frozen.
- Indoor air quality note: if the evaporator coil is dirty or intermittently icing, humidity control suffers and microbial growth risk increases in the drain pan and coil area.
- Prevention: clean condenser coils at least seasonally in dusty environments, inspect evaporator cleanliness annually, verify drains, and record temperature split trends before comfort complaints become severe.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers are not safe to publish from the current data because the exact indoor and outdoor model numbers are missing, and Daikin SkyAir uses multiple thermistor and EEV assemblies across ducted, cassette, and wall-mounted variants.
- For this repair, OEM matters because Daikin thermistors, EEV coils, and control boards are matched to the unit’s control logic and resistance curves. Generic sensors can create false readings and repeat nuisance faults.
- Ask the shop to provide the exact indoor and outdoor model numbers, then the OEM Daikin part number for any proposed thermistor, EEV assembly, or control board. They should also show parts breakdown from Daikin service literature or distributor lookup.
- If a thermistor is failed, OEM is strongly preferred because the board expects a specific resistance-temperature relationship. A close-but-not-exact aftermarket sensor can shift freeze protection thresholds.
- If an EEV is failed, OEM is critical because step count, coil characteristics, and body sizing affect superheat control and compressor protection.
- Pricing sources should include a Daikin distributor, authorized commercial HVAC supplier, or dealer parts department. Avoid online marketplace electronics for sensors and boards unless provenance is clear.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Ask for a line-item quote separating diagnosis, coil cleaning, airflow testing, leak search, refrigerant, and any parts. Bundled pricing hides weak diagnostic logic.
- Use the dirty outdoor coil as leverage: “Before I authorize major parts, I want the condenser cleaned and the system retested under the same ambient conditions.”
- Ask labor-justification questions: “How many hours are you billing for thermistor replacement or EEV replacement, and what access steps make that time necessary on this unit?”
- If refrigerant is proposed, ask: “How many pounds, at what per-pound rate, and what readings proved the charge was low?” A reputable shop will answer directly.
- If they recommend an EEV, ask: “What test ruled out a false CH21 thermistor input causing the valve to hunt?” This forces them to defend the diagnosis with data.
- Walk-away point: any shop that cannot provide model-specific code meaning, measured operating data, and a reasoned sequence from cleaning to testing to repair is not the right shop for an inverter Daikin system.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: refrigerant metering/control problem involving the EEV or its sensor inputs — 76% confidence. Reasoning: noisy expansion valve, short cycling, severe undercooling performance, and CH21 pointing toward freeze-protection/coil-sensing territory fit this best.
- Secondary cause: low refrigerant charge from a leak — 68% confidence. Reasoning: weak cooling and possible evaporator freeze behavior are classic, and low charge can make the EEV noisy or unstable. This remains highly plausible until pressures and superheat/subcooling are measured.
- Tertiary cause: condenser fouling plus airflow deficiency — 55% confidence. Reasoning: the dusty outdoor coil is a confirmed defect and may be materially contributing, but by itself it may not fully explain the CH21 code and valve noise unless paired with indoor airflow issues.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions required: stop using the system as a “run it until it cools” unit. Repeated short cycling stresses the compressor and inverter electronics. Schedule a qualified Daikin-capable commercial HVAC technician promptly.
- Immediate actions required: have the outdoor coil cleaned first, then retest performance at the current ambient. This is the lowest-risk corrective step and removes a major variable from the diagnosis.
- Immediate actions required: require model-specific CH21 interpretation, thermistor testing, airflow/static verification, and refrigerant circuit measurements before authorizing refrigerant or valve replacement.
- Future maintenance schedule: clean condenser coil at least once each cooling season in dusty locations, inspect evaporator coil and blower annually, verify drain operation, and document return/supply split during maintenance visits.
- Warning signs to monitor: visible frost on refrigerant lines or indoor coil, water overflow from thawing ice, louder-than-normal valve chatter, repeated compressor starts every few minutes, or office humidity rising despite the unit running.
- Safety warning: only certified personnel should connect gauges, recover refrigerant, or open electrical compartments. Inverter systems can present dangerous stored electrical energy even after shutdown.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Daikin Applied/Daikin service literature portal and model-specific service manuals for SkyAir indoor/outdoor units. Direct starting point: https://www.daikinac.com/content/resources/manuals/ and authorized distributor service documentation. Use the exact model number to confirm CH21 meaning and thermistor resistance charts.
- Daikin City technical resource portal for service manuals, parts lists, and field support documents: https://www.daikincity.com/ This is directly relevant for obtaining the exact SkyAir service manual, EEV/thermistor diagnostics, and OEM parts lookup by model.
- ACHR News technical archive on superheat, subcooling, airflow, and evaporator freeze diagnostics, useful as an independent trade reference for verifying the low-split/icing/airflow logic: https://www.achrnews.com/topics/2710-refrigeration-service-and-troubleshooting
- HVAC-Talk professional forum discussions on Daikin SkyAir fault interpretation and EEV/thermistor troubleshooting, useful as independent field verification once the exact model is known: https://hvac-talk.com/ Search the exact model plus “CH21” and “thermistor” for technician case histories.
- Specific manufacturer bulletins: no model-specific Daikin bulletin can be responsibly cited from the current data because the exact indoor and outdoor model numbers are missing. Ask the servicing contractor or Daikin distributor to check for service updates related to indoor coil thermistors, EEV control, and freeze-protection faults for your exact 2019 SkyAir model.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize only a proper diagnostic sequence now: retrieve Daikin code history, clean the dusty outdoor coil, verify airflow/static, and record pressures, superheat/subcooling, amp draw, and thermistor readings.
- Do not approve refrigerant, expansion-valve, or compressor replacement until the shop shows model-specific CH21 interpretation and post-cleaning measured data proving the fault.
- If the current shop cannot provide those readings and Daikin-specific documentation, get a second opinion from a contractor experienced with Daikin SkyAir inverter systems.
